Before we start

What your business needs in place.

Nothing here is code, and each one stops a build from starting.

A written feature list

Not a full specification — a list of what the thing does, screen by screen. This is what a fixed price is fixed against, and the reason scope arguments do not happen later.

One person who can decide

Builds stall on unanswered questions far more often than on hard problems. I need one name who can settle a design question inside a day.

Access to whatever it must talk to

Payment gateway, ERP, existing database, a partner's API — with credentials and, ideally, a test environment. An integration promised but not accessible is the most common cause of a missed date.

A real deadline, or none

A date tied to something — a campaign, a tender, a season — changes the build order. An invented deadline just adds pressure without changing decisions, so I would rather know which it is.

Hosting and domains, or permission to buy them

Cloud account, domain, app store accounts if it ships to a store. I can set them all up, but they must be in your name from the first day, not migrated later.

How it runs

Six steps, and you see each one.

  1. 01

    Scope

    We turn the feature list into a screen list and a written scope. The price is fixed against this document.

  2. 02

    Foundations

    Repo, environments, data model, authentication and the deployment pipeline — before any screen is built.

  3. 03

    Build in slices

    Working software every week, on a URL you can open. Not a demo at the end.

  4. 04

    Your review

    You use it on a real device and mark what is wrong. One round of revisions is included.

  5. 05

    Hardening

    Errors, edge cases, loading states, Arabic layout, and the things that only appear under real data.

  6. 06

    Handover

    Repo, credentials, environment docs and a walkthrough. The 30 days start here.

Scope

What this is not, and who it is not for.

These are quoted separately, so the price above stays a price.

  • Ongoing content or data entry
  • Paid marketing and user acquisition
  • Publishing to the app stores — that is its own service
  • Hosting and third-party fees
  • Brand identity design from scratch
  • Legal, tax or compliance advice

Right fit, wrong fit

Saves a call that would end in no.

A good fit

  • You know what the product does, even if not how it looks
  • You want one person accountable for web and mobile together
  • Arabic and English both matter, and RTL has to be right
  • You want to own the code and the accounts at the end
  • You have an unfinished build somebody walked away from

Not a fit

  • You want a price before there is a feature list
  • You need a team of five starting Monday
  • The scope is expected to change weekly
  • You want the cheapest hourly rate on the market

After launch

After it ships.

Software does not stop needing attention the day it ships. Dependencies age out, an OS update breaks a screen, traffic finds the one slow query. Every build includes 30 days; the Care plan keeps a named person on it after that.

Questions

The ones people actually ask.

Can you give a price before the scope is written?

A range, yes; a price, no. The honest version is that a fixed price without a feature list is either padded to cover the unknown or gets renegotiated halfway. Writing the scope is a short paid step and it is yours to take elsewhere.

Why Flutter rather than native iOS and Android?

One codebase, one team, one set of bugs — for the kind of apps most businesses need, native buys very little and costs roughly double. If your app depends on something platform-specific, I will say so and quote native instead.

What happens if it takes longer than planned?

The price is fixed against the written scope, so overrun is mine unless the scope moved. If you add a screen, we price the screen.

Can you finish what someone else started?

Often. It starts with a fixed-price audit that tells you honestly whether finishing it is cheaper than restarting — sometimes the answer is that it is not, and that answer is worth having before more money goes in.

Who owns the code?

You do, from the first commit. It lives in your repo under your account, not mine.
